passage:
Subject: Thank you for asking

Dear Sarita,

I want to tell you why I sent that message before Friday's launch. I was fairly sure the plan was fine, and it would have been easy to leave it there. Instead I asked: "What could make this fail? What am I overlooking?" You replied in ten minutes about the supplier delay in the rainy season, and the two shops with no storage space. I had not thought of either. We changed the delivery dates, and I feel far better about the launch. I'm going to ask those two questions before every plan from now on.

Parveen

qa.q: Which two questions did Parveen ask before the launch?
qa.a: "What could make this fail? What am I overlooking?"

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling about the plan before asking the questions?
qa.a: Fairly confident, and tempted to leave it, though Parveen chose to ask for hidden risks.

qa.q: What did Parveen do with Sarita's answer?
qa.a: Parveen changed the delivery dates to deal with the supplier delay and the shops without storage space.

qa.q: How might Sarita have felt when asked what Parveen was overlooking?
qa.a: Respected and useful, since Sarita replied quickly with two specific risks that Parveen had not considered.

grounding: A thoughtful person asks what would make a plan fail or what they are overlooking, which surfaces hidden risks and shows respect for other viewpoints.

passage:
Interviewer: What is your habit before any event?
Bhavna: I ask two questions out loud: "What could make this fail?" and "What am I overlooking?" I'm Bhavna, and I organise the school annual day. Last year, the plan was perfect on paper. I asked the whole team. Most people said it was fine. Then Vidya, who looks after the ground, said quietly, "The low corner floods if it rains for an hour." I hadn't known. We moved the stage to the higher side and hired a tent. It rained. Nothing was ruined. If I hadn't asked, I would have stood in a puddle in front of two hundred parents. I now notice who tends to stay quiet, and ask them directly.

qa.q: What did Vidya say about the ground?
qa.a: "The low corner floods if it rains for an hour."

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling about the plan before asking the two questions?
qa.a: Confident that the plan was perfect on paper, yet willing to ask for what might be missing.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do after hearing from Vidya?
qa.a: Bhavna moved the stage to the higher side of the ground and hired a tent.

qa.q: How might Vidya have felt when asked directly?
qa.a: Valued, since Vidya knew the ground and spoke up quietly, and the answer saved the event.

grounding: A thoughtful organiser asks what would make the plan fail and what is missing, surfacing a hidden risk from the quiet Vidya.

passage:
I sat across from Reena at the planning meeting for the new school-meal programme in our district. Everyone was excited. Vandana, the senior project lead, had just presented the timeline, and the room was nodding.
Then Reena, who'd joined only three months ago, raised her hand. "Can I ask something? What could make this plan fail?" A few people frowned. Vandana paused. Then she said, slowly, "If the kitchens don't get gas cylinders on time in the monsoon."
The room went quiet. Nobody had planned for that. Someone added, "And if the drivers can't reach the hill schools." For the next half hour, the whole team listed risks and fixes.
I don't know if Reena was nervous. She didn't look it. But after the meeting Vandana stopped by her desk and said, "Keep asking that question."

qa.q: What was the meeting planning?
qa.a: The new school-meal programme in the district.

qa.q: How did Vandana seem to feel about Reena's question by the end?
qa.a: Vandana seemed grateful and impressed, telling Reena to keep asking that question.

qa.q: Why did Reena's question help the team?
qa.a: Asking what would make the plan fail surfaced hidden risks, like gas cylinders in the monsoon, so the team could plan fixes.

qa.q: How might the people who frowned at first see Reena's question later?
qa.a: They would probably see it as useful, since it led to a half hour of important planning.

grounding: Shows a thoughtful colleague asking what would make a plan fail, surfacing hidden risks and showing respect for others' views.

passage:
Monday: Manoj finished the launch plan for the new delivery app and felt proud. Before sending it to the director, he took it to Tanvir from operations. "Can you tell me what I'm not seeing?" Tanvir looked surprised. "Give me a day."
Wednesday: Tanvir came back with a list. "Your plan assumes riders have smartphones with good data. In the outer areas, half don't. And the festival week is when most riders go home." Manoj's stomach dropped. Then he thanked him. They added a phone-call option and moved the launch by a week.
Two weeks later: The launch went smoothly. A rival app launched during the festival and crashed. The director asked Manoj how he'd known. "I asked Tanvir what I was missing," he said.

qa.q: What did Tanvir say half the riders in the outer areas don't have?
qa.a: Smartphones with good data.

qa.q: What did Manoj feel when Tanvir listed the problems?
qa.a: His stomach dropped with worry at first, then he felt grateful and thanked Tanvir.

qa.q: Why did asking 'what am I not seeing?' help the launch?
qa.a: It brought out risks Manoj hadn't thought of, so the team added a phone-call option and moved the launch.

qa.q: How might Tanvir feel about being asked for his view?
qa.a: Tanvir was surprised at first, and probably felt respected and valued for his operations knowledge.

grounding: Shows a colleague asking what they are not seeing, which surfaces hidden risks and respects another's viewpoint.

passage:
"Mridul, you're so pleased with your design, I can see it," said Aparna aunty, smiling. "Let me tell you about my first bridge. I was twenty-five, a junior engineer in the PWD. My design for a small river bridge near Satara was beautiful. I was proud. At the review, my senior, Mr. Kulkarni, asked only one question: 'What could make this fail?'
I was offended. Then I thought about it. The monsoon floods. Tree trunks coming down the river. My pillars were too close together. A big log could jam there and push the whole thing.
I went back and widened the gap. Two years later, a flood came with half a forest in it. The bridge held.
So before you show anyone, ask yourself that question. And ask someone who'll tell you the truth."

qa.q: How old was Aparna aunty when she designed her first bridge?
qa.a: Twenty-five.

qa.q: What was young Aparna feeling when Mr. Kulkarni asked his question?
qa.a: She felt offended and proud of her design at first, then thoughtful as she considered it.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Aparna aunty's story?
qa.a: Mr. Kulkarni's question, which made her see the pillars were too close together, so she widened the gap.

qa.q: How might Mr. Kulkarni have seen young Aparna's design?
qa.a: He probably saw talent but wanted her to check for hidden risks, respecting her enough to ask.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how being asked what would make her design fail surfaced a hidden risk and changed the outcome.

passage: The deck was due to the client at six, and it was already 4:40 when the office power flickered and the backup generator kicked in with a hum. Tejas scrolled fast through the slides: new delivery routes for a bakery chain, three depots, every order dropped by seven the next morning. "Looks done," he said, reaching to send it. Charu held up a hand. "Give me two minutes. What could break this on day one?" Tejas sighed and glanced at the clock. "Nothing. The numbers work." "Then what am I missing? You drove these routes last year." He stopped scrolling. "Actually... the Hosur depot road floods every monsoon. We'd miss the seven o'clock drop for weeks." They added one slide with a backup route and a line about rain delays. At 5:52 the deck went out. The next morning the client's operations head replied that the monsoon slide was the first one she had read closely.

qa.q: At what time did the deck go out?
qa.a: At 5:52 the deck went out.

qa.q: Why did Charu ask "what am I missing" despite the rush?
qa.a: Charu seemed calm but uneasy that a plan checked in a hurry might hide a risk, and respected that Tejas knew the routes better from driving them.

qa.q: What small habit could the team keep from this evening?
qa.a: Before sending any plan, spend two minutes asking what would make it fail, and ask whoever knows the ground best what they see.

qa.q: How might Tejas feel about the question once he remembered the flooding road?
qa.a: He likely felt relieved that the flaw surfaced before sending, and a little valued, because the question was asked on the strength of his own experience.

grounding: Shows Charu, under time pressure, asking what could break a plan and what is being missed, which surfaces a hidden risk and draws on the other person's knowledge.
